analysis.one_liner: Bars Medicare-participating hospitals and clinics from forcing nurses to work beyond scheduled shifts.
analysis.headline: Twenty-nine senators backed the bill, all Democrats, but the Senate Finance Committee never acted on it and it died without a single vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended Medicare rules to stop hospitals, clinics, and home health agencies from requiring nurses to work beyond their scheduled shift — with hard caps of 12 hours in 24 and 80 hours in 14 days. It included a narrow exception for declared emergencies, whistleblower protections for nurses who report violations, fines of up to $10,000 per knowing violation, and public posting of providers fined for breaking the rules. It died in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing, a vote, or any action.
analysis.who_benefits: Nurses at Medicare-participating hospitals, clinics, and home health agencies, who could no longer be forced to work past 12 hours in a day or past their scheduled shift; and patients, whose care is delivered by fatigued nurses less often. The bill's own findings cite research linking higher staffing and rested nurses to better patient outcomes and fewer medical errors [S3]. Nurses who refuse overtime, file complaints, or speak to regulators would be protected from firing, discipline, or retaliation [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits Medicare-participating providers from requiring nurses to work beyond their scheduled shift, more than 12 hours in a 24-hour period, or more than 80 hours in 14 days, with an exception only during a declared state of emergency — and explicitly excludes emergencies caused by a labor dispute or consistent understaffing [S3].

Protects nurses from retaliation — discharge, discipline, loss of promotion, or reporting to state licensing boards — for refusing mandatory overtime or reporting violations, and lets nurses file complaints directly with the Secretary of Health and Human Services, who must investigate [S3].

Imposes civil money penalties of up to $10,000 per knowing violation, with harsher penalties for repeat offenders, and requires HHS to publicly list providers that were fined and what they were fined for [S3].

Requires providers to post nurses' rights notices and schedules, and directs federal studies of safe maximum working hours for nurses and of overtime practices in VA and military medical facilities [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, hospital outpatient departments, critical access hospitals, ambulatory surgical centers, home health agencies, rehabilitation agencies, clinics, and federally qualified health centers that participate in Medicare. These providers had relied on mandatory overtime as a staffing method, as the bill's findings state [S3]. They would have had to hire more staff, use agency nurses, or run at reduced capacity rather than extend nurses' shifts, and would face fines up to $10,000 per knowing violation, with penalties and violations published online [S3].

drawbacks.text: The caps could have constrained hospitals during genuine staffing shortages short of a declared emergency — the bill's own findings acknowledge providers already report substantial difficulty recruiting and retaining nurses, and a facility that cannot fill a shift would have to leave beds unstaffed rather than extend a nurse's shift [S3].
Voluntary overtime would still be allowed, so nurses who needed the pay could keep working long hours; the limits only remove the employer's power to compel it [S3].

Hospitals would bear added staffing costs, which in a Medicare-reimbursed system could put pressure on reimbursement rates or hospital budgets, particularly for rural and critical access hospitals operating on thin margins.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is straightforward: patient safety and nurse working conditions versus hospital staffing costs and scheduling flexibility. The bill was designed narrowly — it caps compelled overtime, not voluntary overtime, and carves out declared emergencies — which addresses the strongest objection that hospitals need flexibility in a nursing shortage. The main honest cost is that short-staffed facilities would have to solve shortages with hiring rather than with fatigue, and some of that cost would land on hospital budgets and potentially on access in rural areas. On balance the design was careful, but it never got far enough for those costs to be examined in a hearing.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which took no action on it for the rest of the Congress, so it died without any vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Edward Kennedy introduced the bill on February 12, 2003, joined by 12 other Democratic senators, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance [S5].
Sixteen additional Democratic senators cosponsored the bill [S4].

The full action history shows no committee hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no Senate floor action after the referral; the next recorded action after introduction and referral is nothing [S5].
The bill was never enacted and never received a vote in either chamber during the 108th Congress, which ended January 3, 2005 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare-participating hospitals and other providers that used mandatory overtime to staff shifts came out ahead: they avoided federal overtime caps, retaliation protections, and fines of up to $10,000 per violation, and kept the staffing flexibility the bill would have restricted. Nurses and patients gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hospitals that rely on mandatory overtime

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat — 29 senators in all — and no Republican supported the bill; it died in a committee chaired by a Republican without any recorded action.

industries.note: The bill capped mandatory overtime at 12 hours per day and 80 per 14 days for hospitals, clinics, home health agencies, and similar Medicare providers, with fines up to $10,000 per knowing violation. These providers had relied on compelled overtime as a staffing method; ending that practice would have forced them to hire more nurses at real cost, which is why the bill's death preserved their existing staffing model.

Nurses would have gained enforceable limits on compelled overtime, retaliation protections, and a federal complaint process. The bill's findings say job dissatisfaction and forced overtime are pushing roughly 500,000 licensed nurses out of practice, so the limits also aimed at keeping nurses in the profession — which benefits patients.
